title: Quantifying the Protective Effect of Cryocooling on Electron Beam-Induced Radiolytic Damage via Impact Crater Expansion
content: Electron microscopy has been unilaterally revolutionized by the ability to conduct imaging and diffraction experiments at cryogenic temperatures. Nevertheless, the exact mechanistic origins underpinning cryocooling’s mitigation of electron beam-induced radiolytic damage remain unclear. Previously, using ambient-temperature scanning nanobeam electron diffraction [1], we demonstrated that repeated irradiation of organic and organometallic nanocrystals at a single probe position leads to the concentric propagation of radiolytic damage hundreds of nm beyond the initial point of exposure—phenomena we termed “impact craters” [2]. Here we apply 4D-STEM at ambient (295 K), liquid-nitrogen (95 K), and liquid-helium (25 K) [3] temperatures to record dual-space movies of nanocrystalline p-terphenyl (C18H14) at consecutive stages of radiolytic decay. We show that the tides of amorphization previously observed only at RT expand approximately 4× more slowly at 95 K relative to 295 K. Under analogous irradiation conditions at 25 K, impact crater expansion is unobservable. We also demonstrate that perdeuteration of the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon scaffold [4] leads to a kinetic isotope effect in which delocalization of radiolytic damage is slowed by a lesser protective factor of approximately √2, consistent with the ratio between the vibrational frequencies of the sp2 C-H and C-D bonds measured by infrared spectroscopy [5]. These results establish the impact crater method as a powerful mechanistic probe for quantifying the consequences of radiolytic damage at variable temperatures. [6]
